basic_info.name: HAPI FHIR
basic_info.description: HAPI FHIR is the reference open-source Java implementation of the HL7 FHIR standard, providing a complete toolchain - object model and parser/serialiser, client, plain REST server, a production JPA persistence server, an instance validator, version converters, terminology services and a CLI - across FHIR DSTU1, DSTU2, DSTU2.1, DSTU3, R4, R4B and R5. The single most load-bearing fact for MediKiosk Module C is that it is the de facto Java validation and persistence layer for ABDM/NRCeS work in India: the NRCeS FHIR IG for ABDM (ndhm.in, current published release v6.5.0, 2025-05-08) is an NPM package that HAPI can install and validate against, so a HAPI instance can check that an emitted OPConsultRecord/Bundle actually conforms to the Indian IG rather than only to base FHIR R4. It is Apache-2.0, maintained by Smile Digital Health (Toronto) - originally created at University Health Network by James Agnew - with commercial support sold through Smile CDR, and a public test server at hapi.fhir.org. Current release line as of 2026-09: v8.12.1 (2026-09-15), v8.12.0 (2026-09-01), v8.10.1 (2026-07-22), v8.10.0 (2026-05-21), with documentation building toward 8.14.0. Minimum Java is now JDK 17 (Java 11 support was dropped), Java 21 is supported. It is heavyweight JVM infrastructure, not a kiosk runtime: on a ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk it belongs as an offline/build-time validator or clinic-side server, not as a process running on the patient terminal.
basic_info.organization: Maintained by Smile Digital Health (Toronto, Canada); the project originated at the University Health Network (UHN) and was created by James Agnew. Commercial support is offered via Smile CDR. Contributions come from a large community (roughly 270+ contributors; top committers include jamesagnew, tadgh, fil512 and other Smile engineers).
basic_info.country: Canada (Smile Digital Health, Toronto). Used worldwide, including extensively in Indian ABDM/NRCeS implementations.
basic_info.status: Production, actively and heavily maintained. GitHub metrics at verification: ~2.4k stars, ~1.5k forks, 139 watchers, 11,011 commits, 122 releases, with a steady patch/codename cadence (8.6.x 'Euphoria', 8.8.0 'Prologue', 8.10.x, 8.12.x). The latest tagged release v8.12.1 shipped on 2026-09-15, one day before verification, confirming current active development. A public demo/test server runs at hapi.fhir.org and is still referenced in the docs.

technical_features.what_it_does: HAPI FHIR gives a Java/JVM project everything needed to produce, consume, validate and persist FHIR. The model layer (hapi-fhir-base plus version-specific hapi-fhir-structures-* modules) provides typed resource classes, a fluent API, JSON and XML parsers/serialisers, profile/extension handling, version converters and a Bundle builder. The client layer provides generic/fluent and annotation-based REST clients over Apache HttpClient 5 or OkHttp. The server layer offers a 'plain' REST server and, more importantly for ABDM, a JPA server (hapi-fhir-jpaserver, Spring Boot starter) that stores resources in a relational database (H2, PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, MS SQL Server, Oracle up to 23ai), performs FHIR search, and exposes terminology operations ($validate-code, $expand, $translate). The validation layer (hapi-fhir-validation + FhirInstanceValidator, schema/Schematron validators, RepositoryValidatingInterceptor) validates resources against base FHIR and against any loaded profiles. Critically for Module C, HAPI can install FHIR NPM Implementation Guide packages - including NRCeS's ndhm.in - via NpmPackageValidationSupport / the JPA PackageInstallerSvcImpl and the implementationguides configuration block, so validation can be performed against the ABDM profiles (OPConsultRecord, DocumentBundle, Patient, Practitioner, Organization, etc.) rather than only base R4. It also ships HL7 IPS support, MDM (master data management/deduplication), Batch2 bulk operations, partitioning/multitenancy, a ConsentInterceptor, BALP audit logging and a standalone CLI.
technical_features.architecture: Modular Maven multi-project (roughly 30+ modules). Core: hapi-fhir-base (no-dependency core used even on Android), hapi-fhir-structures-{dstu2,dstu2.1,dstu3,r4,r4b,r5}, hapi-fhir-converter (cross-version conversion). Networking: hapi-fhir-client, hapi-fhir-client-apache-http5, hapi-fhir-client-okhttp. Servers: hapi-fhir-server (plain), hapi-fhir-jpaserver-base + hapi-fhir-storage + hapi-fhir-jpa (JPA/Hibernate persistence, search parameters, subscriptions, MDM, batch2, partitioning, HFQL), hapi-fhir-jpaserver-ips (International Patient Summary), hapi-fhir-jpaserver-starter (Spring Boot). Validation: hapi-fhir-validation plus hapi-fhir-validation-resources-{r4,r4b,r5,...}. Tooling: hapi-fhir-cli (including migrate-database and validation commands), hapi-fhir-typescript (generated TS definitions). The validator's underlying engine is the HL7 org.hl7.fhir.core validator (published separately as validator_cli.jar), which is what most ABDM projects actually run for IG validation. Build requires Maven, JDK 17+ (21 supported) and Lombok.
technical_features.inputs: For validation: FHIR R4/R5 resources and Bundles as JSON or XML, the FHIR version, and loaded conformance resources (base definitions plus NPM IG packages such as ndhm.in). For the JPA server: POST/PUT/PATCH/transaction Bundle submissions, search queries, terminology operations. For the client: a FHIR base URL, OAuth/SMART credentials and resource bodies. HAPI itself is content-agnostic - it does not ingest patient dialogue, audio, documents or vitals semantics; it only sees already-structured FHIR.
technical_features.outputs: Validated or rejected FHIR resources with an OperationOutcome containing errors/warnings/expression paths; parsed/serialised JSON or XML; persisted resources in a relational store with version history; search Bundles; expanded or translated ValueSets/ConceptMaps; converted resources between FHIR versions; CapabilityStatements and OpenAPI/Swagger descriptions. For Module C the relevant output is a pass/fail + OperationOutcome when validating an emitted OPConsultRecord DocumentBundle against the NRCeS ndhm.in package - not a clinical summary itself.
technical_features.standards_compliance: HAPI implements and tracks the HL7 FHIR specification across DSTU1, DSTU2, DSTU2.1, DSTU3, R4 (4.0.1), R4B (4.3.0) and R5 (5.0.0) - so FHIR R4, which ABDM mandates, is a first-class supported line. Validation is real and machine-checked: base-spec conformance is built in, and profile/IG conformance is achieved by loading the relevant NPM package (e.g. NRCeS ndhm.in v6.5.0) so the validator enforces the Indian profiles' mandatory fields and bindings rather than just base R4. It also supports HL7 International Patient Summary (IPS) profiles, SMART on FHIR scope enforcement, BALP audit, and terminology systems including LOINC, SNOMED CT, ICD-10-CM and UCUM via built-in/loadable resources. Important caveats: NRCeS conformance is a property of the loaded ndhm.in package, not of HAPI itself, and full SNOMED CT/LOINC terminology checking needs a terminology server or the relevant expanded resources configured, otherwise terminology checks are skipped. HAPI's documentation does not itself claim ABDM/NRCeS certification; it is the transportable validator, and NRCeS/ABDM projects load the Indian package on top.
technical_features.offline_capability: HAPI is fully self-hostable and needs no cloud service: the JPA server runs on a local/on-prem relational database and the validation engine runs entirely locally once the base definitions and any IG packages are present in the local package cache. This makes it compatible with MediKiosk's offline-first and India data-residency constraints - the ndhm.in package and validation can be vendored locally, and the JPA store can be a local PostgreSQL/H2. The main offline consideration is packaging: the initial Maven dependencies and IG packages must be bundled/downloaded once, and the JVM + JPA server footprint is significant. There is no built-in store-and-forward sync; that would be the kiosk/HIS layer's responsibility.
technical_features.languages_supported: Not a natural-language tool. HAPI/FHIR carry multilingual content as ordinary strings (e.g. CodeableConcept.text, Narrative, Communication, or the FHIR translation extension), so Hindi/Devanagari or Hinglish content can be stored and exchanged but receives no special tokenisation, transliteration or bilingual-rendering support from HAPI. [uncertain] No AYUSH-specific or Indic-script behaviour beyond generic FHIR string handling was found.
technical_features.deployment_model: Any JVM deployment: library embedded in a Spring Boot / Jakarta app, standalone JAR/WAR plain server, the hapi-fhir-jpaserver-starter (Spring Boot) as a full FHIR repository, or containerised. Backends include H2 (embedded) through PostgreSQL/MySQL/MSSQL/Oracle for production. Requires JDK 17 minimum (Java 21 supported); Android is targeted at API level 34 via the base module. No GPU is needed (validation and persistence are CPU/IO-bound). No published minimum RAM/CPU figures, but the JPA server plus JVM and a relational database realistically needs more headroom than a constrained ~4GB kiosk comfortably offers alongside the kiosk application - the sensible split is a build-time/pre-deploy validation job or a clinic/HIS-side server, with only lightweight emitted JSON on the kiosk itself.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: HAPI is not a model, so there are no accuracy/F1/ROUGE figures; its quality signal is spec-conformance and test coverage rather than clinical correctness. Codecov coverage is published, there is a very large R4/R4B/R5/DSTU2/DSTU3 test suite, and conformance correctness is demonstrated by passing the FHIR specification's own tests and by use in HL7 connectathons and national programmes. Per-release changelogs are detailed and enumerate fixes, which is itself an indicator of active correctness maintenance.
performance_metrics.latency: No official latency/throughput benchmark for the server is published on the main site, though a dedicated JPA performance documentation page covers search and scaling guidance. Individual changelog entries report performance work (e.g. batching parallel loading of externally stored resources during search, removing an expensive JOIN on resource update, a more efficient search-results SQL query for resources with long version history, and indexed full-text/refchain optimisations). Treat any specific ms/throughput claim as workload-specific; HAPI is generally considered production-scalable but heavier than purpose-built lightweight stores.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: The library is pure Java with no GPU requirement - appropriate for CPU-only environments in principle. Minimum runtime is JDK 17 (Java 21 supported); Java 11 support was dropped. The JPA server additionally needs a relational database and JVM heap, and dependency tree is large (Spring Boot, Hibernate, Jackson, Thymeleaf optional, Schematron optional). Smile does not publish a hard RAM/CPU minimum. For the ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk this is a caution: bundling a full JPA server onto the kiosk is likely excessive, whereas running the lighter validator (or the validator_cli.jar from org.hl7.fhir.core, which is the same core engine) in a build/CI or clinic-side step is cheap. Store only the emitted JSON at the kiosk.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Community/adoption scale at verification: ~2.4k GitHub stars, ~1.5k forks, 139 watchers, ~270 contributing developers, 11,011 commits and 122 releases. It is one of the two dominant open-source FHIR implementations (alongside Firely/.NET) and is widely used deep in national health programmes; in India it is repeatedly cited as the Java stack for ABDM HMIS/EMR work and for NRCeS-profile validation. These are repository/popularity metrics rather than deployed-transaction volumes; HAPI does not publish server transaction or install counts.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Quality is established by standards-conformance testing rather than human or ML evaluation: comprehensive unit/integration test suites per FHIR version, the FHIR specification's own validator test cases, codecov-tracked coverage, continuous Azure Pipelines builds (main + SNAPSHOT + release pipelines), and participation in HL7 connectathons. Changelogs record issue-by-issue fixes with linked HAPI/issue numbers. There is no peer-reviewed clinical evaluation and none is applicable; the relevant verification for Module C is whether the ndhm.in package loads and the ABDM profile validation produces the expected OperationOutcome on known-good and known-bad bundles.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: HAPI FHIR is the reference tool MediKiosk should use to prove that its emitted OPConsultRecord/DocumentBundle is actually NRCeS-conformant, not merely R4-shaped. Because the NRCeS FHIR IG for ABDM is distributed as an NPM package (ndhm.in, current published v6.5.0, 2025-05-08) and HAPI can install and validate against NPM IG packages, a HAPI validator instance gives Module C a deterministic, offline-capable conformance gate: load ndhm.in, validate the bundle, and fail the build on any OperationOutcome error. This directly supports the 'NRCeS-conformant emission' and 'physician attestation' differentiators by removing hand-waving about whether the summary would be accepted. HAPI is also the natural persistence/search layer if the summary is ever stored as FHIR on the clinic or HIS side, and its terminology services could host SNOMED CT India / CDCI / AYUSH Extension ValueSets for offline code validation. It supplies no elicitation, no summarisation, no document OCR and no AYUSH-specific logic - it is strictly the interoperability substrate under Module C.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) HAPI's validator - or the identical org.hl7.fhir.core validator_cli.jar that HAPI wraps - as the mandatory conformance gate in Module C's pipeline and CI, configured with -version 4.0.1 and -ig against the ndhm.in package, because ABDM will reject malformed FHIR and base-R4-only validation misses India-specific mandatory fields; (2) the NPM package/IG-install mechanism to vendor the NRCeS package locally for offline validation; (3) HAPI as the candidate FHIR store/terminology server on the clinic/HIS side (not on the kiosk) if the summary must persist as queryable FHIR; (4) its ConsentInterceptor/BALP patterns as design references for ABDM consent and audit. Reject or adapt: (1) running the full HAPI JPA server on the ~4GB kiosk - the JVM + Spring + database footprint is disproportionate, and offline-first with a single kiosk does not need a FHIR search server; (2) assuming HAPI or the FHIR Validator will catch AYUSH terminology problems - it will not, because NAMASTE is not bound into the ABDM IG, so AYUSH coding correctness needs a separate rule/terminology layer; (3) treating 'validates against base R4' as sufficient - the NRCeS package must be loaded or the validation is not ABDM-relevant; (4) depending on a live remote terminology server for SNOMED/LOINC checks at a disconnected site - pre-expand/vendor terminology or accept skipped terminology checks.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: HAPI is heavyweight JVM infrastructure with a JDK 17+ floor and a large dependency tree, so it does not fit naturally on the resource-constrained kiosk and should be positioned off-device. NRCeS conformance is not intrinsic: it depends on downloading and loading the ndhm.in package, and there are documented practical frictions around IG packages - the NRCeS package URL may change or be unavailable (the examples repository explicitly warns to download manually if the package URL fails), and HAPI's package installation can fail on malformed packages or partitioned servers (multiple such bugs are in the 8.x changelogs). Full SNOMED CT/LOINC validation needs a terminology server or expanded resources, otherwise terminology checks are silently skipped, which could give false confidence. HAPI provides no AYUSH/NAMASTE/ICD-11 TM2 awareness, no Prakriti/Vikriti handling, no summarisation and no elicitation. Version currency is a minor risk in the other direction: release numbering is non-monotonic across branches (e.g. an 8.6.8 patch after 8.8.0), which can confuse dependency pinning, and the docs site sometimes shows a SNAPSHOT version. Finally, while Apache-2.0 makes the library itself freely usable, there is no free commercial support - production support is a paid Smile CDR proposition.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: HAPI is infrastructure, not a competitor, and it strengthens rather than erodes MediKiosk's differentiation on the NRCeS-conformant-emission and India-residency axes: it is the open, self-hostable, offline-capable validation/persistence layer that makes 'we emit NRCeS-conformant bundles' a testable claim and keeps data processing on Indian soil. It does nothing on the axes where MediKiosk differentiates - it neither elicits history, nor summarises, nor digitises documents, nor handles AYUSH clinical content, nor bilingual rendering, nor physician attestation. The one nuance worth stating: HAPI makes standards-compliance table stakes, not a moat - any ABDM entrant can validate with it - so MediKiosk's defensibility must remain in the elicitation-to-structured-summary layer and in how it resolves the AYUSH/Prakriti gap the ABDM IG leaves open, with HAPI used as the assurance mechanism underneath.

business_info.license: Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0), confirmed by the LICENSE.txt/LICENSE badge in the repository and the project's own license page. Permissive: free for commercial and closed-source use with attribution, no network-copyleft obligation. Note that some bundled components have their own notices (e.g. LOINC_NOTES.txt, NOTICE.txt), and the underlying HL7 validator engine is likewise open source.
business_info.pricing: The library and servers are free and open source with no fee. Commercial support, SLAs and enterprise features are sold separately through Smile Digital Health's Smile CDR product; there is no charge for HAPI FHIR itself.
business_info.funding: Commercially backed by Smile Digital Health, which funds ongoing development as the open-source core underpinning its paid Smile CDR platform; the project originated at University Health Network (academic/health-system origin). No external venture round specific to HAPI FHIR was found. [uncertain] Detailed corporate financials were not researched.
business_info.commercial_status: Open-source project with a commercial-support business model (open core). It is a free community tool, professionally maintained by a company that monetises the surrounding enterprise platform.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: Direct FHIR implementation alternatives: Firely (Firely .NET SDK / Server / Vonk, Netherlands), Microsoft FHIR Server for Azure, Google Cloud Healthcare API (FHIR), Amazon HealthLake, Medplum (TS), Smile CDR (HAPI's own commercial superset), Blaze (Java, performance-focused), IBM/LinuxForHealth FHIR Server, and Spark/Firely Server. For validation specifically, the HL7 org.hl7.fhir.core validator_cli.jar is the canonical engine and is the same underlying core HAPI wraps; ahdis/matchbox is a fork of the HAPI JPA starter specialised for validation/mapping and is the closest direct competitor in the validation niche. In the ABDM/India context, the practical 'validation layer' competitors are matchbox and the standalone HL7 validator CLI.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: HAPI integrates with any FHIR R4/R5 endpoint and with the FHIR NPM package registry, through which the NRCeS ndhm.in ABDM IG package is installed for India-specific validation. It supports SMART on FHIR (scope enforcement), HL7 International Patient Summary, BALP audit logging, CDS Hooks, CQL/clinical reasoning, and the HAPI JPA starter. In India it is used across ABDM-oriented HMIS/EMR projects and is named in developer guidance as the Java stack for building and validating ABDM bundles; third-party repos (e.g. Nirmitee abdm-fhir-bundle-examples, VenuAjitesh/FHIR-Mapper) pair HAPI with the ndhm.in package and validator_cli for NRCeS-profile validation of OPConsultation, Prescription, DischargeSummary, DiagnosticReport and HealthDocumentRecord bundles. It does not integrate with NAMASTE directly.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: HAPI is one of the two anchors of the open FHIR tooling ecosystem (the other being Firely/.NET), so choosing it is low-risk and well-precedented, with abundant examples, books, and community support including a Google Group and chat.fhir.org. The ABDM ecosystem is explicitly FHIR R4 document-Bundle based, and the standard Indian practice is to validate emitted bundles with the HL7 validator against the NRCeS IG - HAPI aligns exactly with that practice, which is a procurement/credibility tailwind. The main ecosystem risk is that ABDM/NRCeS package distribution is not fully reliable (package URLs change, registry availability varies), so HAPI-based validation pipelines must vendor the IG package rather than fetch it live. Also relevant: HAPI's commercial guardian Smile CDR means the open core is strategically maintained; this is generally healthy but means enterprise-grade support is a paid dependency if MediKiosk ever productionises a HAPI-based server.

history.release_date: 2014-06-24 (the hapifhir/hapi-fhir GitHub repository was created then; the project began at University Health Network and pre-dates the GitHub mirror). It has been the leading Java FHIR implementation since the DSTU era.
history.key_milestones: 2014: repository/project origin, early FHIR DSTU support. Through 2014-2020: progressive support for DSTU1/DSTU2/DSTU2.1/DSTU3/R4 and growth of the JPA server, validator and client modules; commercial backing via Smile CDR. 2020-2023: R4B and R5 support, MDM, Batch2, partitioning, IPS support, CLI maturity. 7.0.0 era: Jakarta namespace migration (Java EE to Jakarta) and Java 11 baseline. 2024: 7.4.x/7.6.x releases, database schema changes (RES_TYPE_ID), ongoing search/performance work. 2025: 8.2.0 moved the minimum to JDK 17 (Java 11 dropped, Android API 34); 8.6.0 'Euphoria' (Nov 2025) with package-install and reindex changes; 8.6.x patch line through early 2026. 2026: 8.8.0 'Prologue' (Feb 2026) with Consent REJECT now blocking writes and an MSSQL case-sensitivity migration; 8.10.0 (May 2026); 8.12.0 (Sep 2026); 8.12.1 (15 Sep 2026).
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: In the Mar-Sep 2026 window HAPI shipped a steady release cadence. v8.8.0 'Prologue' (2026-02-19) is the headline change just inside/at the window edge: it makes a Consent REJECT abort write operations (POST/PUT/PATCH return 403) instead of leaving the database inconsistent, adds a database migration for case-sensitive FHIR IDs on MSSQL (which breaks zero-downtime upgrade for a subset of users, with a documented --skip-versions workaround), enables database-stored CodeSystem/ValueSet resources to override built-in HL7 definitions via JpaStorageSettings.setAllowDatabaseValidationOverride, extends merge/undo-merge to any resource type, adds bulk-patch and _includeHistory to $export, refactors $reindex onto Batch2, adds Oracle 23ai support, fixes FHIRPath constants for R4, and improves search/validation performance (parallel loading of externally stored resources, removed JOINs, better SQL). v8.10.0 (2026-05-21) and v8.10.1 (2026-07-22) followed, and v8.12.0/v8.12.1 (2026-09-01/15) are the current head, all with detailed changelogs. No change in this window affects the ABDM/NRCeS use case adversely; the ConsentInterceptor write-rejection change is actually a behaviour Module C should note if it uses consent enforcement.

market_positioning.target_users: Java/JVM developers and health-IT engineers building FHIR clients, servers, validators or clinical applications; national digital-health programmes and HIS/EMR vendors (including ABDM/NRCeS implementers in India); and enterprises needing a self-hosted FHIR repository. Secondary users include the open-source community and HL7 connectathon participants. It is developer/integrator infrastructure, not an end-user product.
market_positioning.market_segment: FHIR tooling / interoperability middleware and FHIR server engines - the implementation layer beneath ABDM, EHR and health-data-exchange products. It is not an intake, ambient-scribing, PHR, AYUSH-software or diagnostics-kiosk product.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: HAPI FHIR positions itself as 'HAPI FHIR - Java API for HL7 FHIR Clients and Servers' and 'an open-source implementation of the FHIR specification in Java', with the pitch that it handles the heavy lifting of FHIR so teams can focus on their application, and that commercial support is available through Smile CDR. Its documentation promotes it as the reference toolkit for parsing, validating, storing and exchanging FHIR across R4/R5, with a public demo server at hapi.fhir.org for experimentation.
